title: Fixed-Size Arrays — std::array
summary: `std::array<T, N>` is an array whose length `N` is fixed at **compile time**. It cannot grow, needs no separate memory block, and can be `constexpr`. Use it when the count never changes.
markdown:
## When the size never changes Seven days in a week. Nine squares on a noughts-and-crosses board. Fifty-two cards. When the number of elements is fixed for ever, `std::array` states that in the type. ``` std::vector v{ 1, 2, 3 }; std::array a{ 1, 2, 3 }; [pointer|size|capacity] ──▶ [1|2|3] [1|2|3] the vector itself a separate the elements are block elsewhere the array itself ``` A vector holds a pointer to elements stored elsewhere. A `std::array` **is** its elements, with nothing extra. | | `std::vector` | `std::array` | |---|---|---| | Size decided | While running; can change | At compile time; fixed | | Where the elements live | A separately allocated block | Inside the array object | | `push_back` | Yes | No | | Can be `constexpr` | Limited | Yes | | Header | `` | `` | ## Using one ```cpp #include #include int main() { std::array primes{ 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 }; std::array zeros{}; // 0.0 0.0 0.0 primes[0] = 1; std::cout << primes.size() << ' ' << primes.at(4) << '\n'; // 5 11 for (int p : primes) { std::cout << p << ' '; } std::cout << zeros.size() << '\n'; return 0; } ``` The second template argument is the length. Everything you know from vectors that does not change the size works the same way: `[]`, `at`, `size`, `front`, `back` and range-based loops. ## Lookup tables at compile time A `constexpr` array is a table the compiler builds into the program. ```cpp constexpr std::array daysInMonth{ 31, 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31 }; static_assert(daysInMonth[1] == 28); // verified during the build ``` Reading from it at run time is a single memory access, and using it in other `constexpr` code costs nothing at all. ### Indexing with an enum Combine the `count` idiom from [[4.05 Enums]] with an array to get a table with named slots. ```cpp enum class Stat { strength, dexterity, intellect, count }; std::array(Stat::count)> stats{ 10, 14, 8 }; stats[static_cast(Stat::dexterity)] += 2; ``` The casts are the price of `enum class` not converting silently. A small helper function that does the cast tidies it up. ## Passing arrays to functions The length is part of the type. `std::array` and `std::array` are as different as `int` and `double`. ```cpp void print(const std::array& values); // accepts length 5 only ``` To accept any length, make the length a template parameter: ```cpp template void printAny(const std::array& values) { for (const auto& x : values) { std::cout << x << ' '; } std::cout << '\n'; } ``` `N` here is a **non-type template parameter**: a value, not a type, that is fixed at compile time. They get a full treatment in [[9.02 Non-Type Parameters and Template Specialization]]. ## Arrays of structs ```cpp struct Planet { std::string_view name{}; double gravity{}; }; constexpr std::array planets{ { { "Mercury", 3.7 }, { "Earth", 9.8 }, { "Mars", 3.7 }, } }; ``` Note the **double braces**. The outer pair is for the `std::array`, and the inner pair is for the plain array it wraps. With simple element types the compiler lets you omit one pair; with structs you need both. ## Which container? ```mermaid flowchart TD Q{"Is the number of elements
known at compile time
and never going to change?"} -- yes --> A["std::array"] Q -- no --> V["std::vector"] ``` When in doubt, use a vector. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Can you `push_back` onto a `std::array`? - Yes, like a vector + No, its length is fixed at compile time - Yes, but only up to twice its size - Only if it was declared `constexpr` > A `std::array` has a fixed length that is part of its type. For a growing list, use `std::vector`. ? Why choose `std::array` over `std::vector`? - It can grow faster than a vector - It checks every index automatically + Its size is fixed, it needs no heap allocation, and it suits `constexpr` - It is the only standard container that can hold structs > When the size never changes, `std::array` avoids a heap allocation and can be used at compile time. ? Are `std::array` and `std::array` the same type? - Yes, both are arrays of `int` - Yes, the length is only a starting size + No, the length is part of the type > The length is a template argument, so the two are different types. A function taking one cannot take the other. ? Why do arrays of structs need double braces? - To make each struct `const` - The outer braces are optional decoration - One pair per member of the struct + One pair for the `std::array`, one for the array inside it > `std::array` wraps a built-in array, so the outer braces are for the `std::array` and the inner ones for the array inside it. ```
ideas:
1. Make a `constexpr std::array` of month names and print the name for a month number.
2. Store seven daily temperatures and print the name of the hottest day.
3. Write a template `sum` that works for a `std::array` of any element type and length.

cards.a:
No, its length is fixed at compile time

A `std::array` has a fixed length that is part of its type. For a growing list, use `std::vector`.

Its size is fixed, it needs no heap allocation, and it suits `constexpr`

When the size never changes, `std::array` avoids a heap allocation and can be used at compile time.

No, the length is part of the type

The length is a template argument, so the two are different types. A function taking one cannot take the other.

cards.q: Why do arrays of structs need double braces?
cards.a:
One pair for the `std::array`, one for the array inside it

`std::array` wraps a built-in array, so the outer braces are for the `std::array` and the inner ones for the array inside it.
